new_statements.quote: 4.2.1 Although tone is phonemic in Huli, it carries a low functional load. [...] 4.2.3 However, a point of near unanimity is that there are indeed four contrasting tones, which are: Tone 1 (falling) [...] Tone 2 (rising) [...] Tone 3 (level) [...] Tone 4 (rising-falling) [...] 4.3.4.1 Generally, at least one accented syllable in an information unit is given prominence, and this can be another source of tone perturbation. [...] 4.3.4.2 However, when more than one information unit occurs in an utterance, a speaker will typically accord salience to the one that he/she wishes to foreground. This is achieved by stepping up the pitch and increasing the loudness of the prominent syllable of that unit, other units being given a secondary prominence.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Huli is a tone language (Lomas: four contour tonemes, falling / rising / level / rising-falling, with low functional load and inconsistent use across speakers; SIL 1992 OPD and Pugh-Kitingan 2011: three word-tones, high-falling / mid-level / low-rising). Lomas gives no rule placing stress on a particular syllable of the word: prominence ('accent', 'primary stress' in his caret notation) is assigned at the level of the intonational information unit -- at least one accented syllable per unit, and the foregrounded unit's prominent syllable gets extra pitch and loudness (primary stress) while other units get secondary prominence. Stress appears in his segmental rules only as a conditioning feature ([+STRESS] in vowel allophony, 3.8.1.5, 3.11) and in the OPD only as 'certain non-stressed syllables' (p. 4); neither source states which syllable of a word is stressed.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Lomas 1988 p. 83: when several information units occur in an utterance, the non-foregrounded units are 'given a secondary prominence' (phrase-level, not word-level).
new_statements.exceptions: Lomas 1988 p. 77: tones 'are not employed in a uniform or consistent manner across the language group. Some speakers do not use pitch to discriminate between certain homophones, while others do'; tones are perturbed in connected speech by intonation contours and by prominence (pp. 82-84). SIL OPD p. 3: 'The functional load of contrastive tone is not very high.'
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level: tone (lexical, contrasting monosyllabic and disyllabic diads/triads such as i 'you sg.' vs i 'I', hale 'ear'/'tree sp.'/'torch', ma 'taro'/'neck'/'let's go'). Stress/accent statement is phrase-level only (information unit in connected speech, mingographic data); no citation-form or word-domain stress rule is given in any opened source.
new_statements.identity_note: Sources describe Huli proper (huli1244). Lomas 1988 surveyed tone across 22 Huli locations (35 speakers) and bases the intonation/prominence description "mainly on data from the Gumu area" (a Huli dialect area, no separate glottocode); the SIL 1992 OPD is checked by "an expatriate speaker of Huli"; Pugh-Kitingan and the Rules worked at Tari. No differently named variety involved.

sources.note: Ch. 3 segmental phonology (pp. 20-75) uses [+STRESS] as a conditioning feature in vowel-allophony rules (3.8.1.5, 3.11) but never states where stress falls; ch. 4 Prosodies: tone is phonemic, four contour tonemes, low functional load, inconsistent across speakers (4.2, p. 77); intonation 4.3: at least one accented syllable per information unit is given prominence; foregrounded unit gets primary stress by raised pitch and loudness, others secondary prominence (4.3.4.1-2, pp. 82-83); Appendix A tone survey (mingograms) mentions only mora prominence in diphthongs. No word-stress placement rule.

sources.note: p. 75 n. 2: grave = words uttered on a falling tone, acute = rising tones, macron = level tones; 'Since tone is perturbed in the singing of bi te', sung texts carry no diacritics. p. 83: 'the tonal system of spoken Huli impacts on its melodic structure' (citing Pugh-Kitingan 1981:332, 335-36). Nothing on stress.

sources.note: p. 115: 'Huli is a tone language that has three contrastive word-tones: low-rising, high-falling, and mid-level.. with sentence-terminating intonation producing a fall on verb affixes at the end of statements (Rule 1977:10; Rule and Rule 1970a:x-xi).' Footnote 7: tone marks are written on the first syllable 'although the pitch patterns marked by them pertain to the word as a whole.' Also states the Huli have no concepts of metre and rhythm; speech-tone determines melodic shape. No mention of stress.
